LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) -- He is the international superstar responsible for breathing life into the iconic comic book hero Wolverine. Her movies have earned more than $2 billion worldwide, including the entire "X-Men" franchise. Hugh Jackman emerges as Wolverine in "X-Men Origins: Wolverine," which opened Friday. Actor Hugh Jackman and film producer Lauren Shuler Donner recently sat down for a candid conversation about their new film, "X-Men Origins: Wolverine." Specifically, the pair talked about the scene in which Jackman's character is transformed from a simple mutant with bony claws that periodically protrude from the back of his hands to an invincible mutant filled with an indestructible metal called adamantium. This scene represents the ultimate birth of a comic legend as the character is transformed from Logan to Wolverine.  Watch the scene in which Wolverine is unleashed » . Hugh Jackman: I knew this was the birth of the character; this is where we see him in full flight. It's called in the comic book "berserker rage." It's not really in the English language, but it may be now! But, this idea that this complete animal [has been] unleashed, which is obviously the entire story -- this battle between the animal and human is something we all relate to. Lauren Shuler Donner: There were many things he had to do in the tank, you know. One of them was he had to be lowered, and then the needles had to come towards him. Now, most of those were CGI, so he had to look in certain places where the needles were. But, he couldn't hear [director] Gavin [Hood]. So they ... tried all kinds of sounds, speakers, everything. ... They finally devised this toe method where, if Gavin pulled on Hugh's big toe, it meant the things are coming, the second toe is this, the last toe is rise up, very sophisticated. (laughter) Jackman: I had in my head that I've got to be in much better shape -- not better shape, different shape, kind of ridiculous shape because I wanted it to be uncomfortable. I wanted it to feel like I felt when I saw Robert De Niro in "Cape Fear," that -- whoa, this guy is dangerous, he's powerful, he's dangerous, and he can snap at any point. Donner: There's an iconic drawing of Wolverine coming out of the tank in the comics with the things popping out of him and his hair all over him in a rage, and we wanted to be that image. That's the image we wanted for the fans. Jackman: I was a little frightened when I watched it, like, "Is that me?" [My wife] Deb was like, "Hugh, this is ridiculous. I don't even know who that is."

LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) — He is the international superstar who brought the iconic comic-book hero Wolverine to life. She is the producer whose films—including the entire “X-Men” franchise—have earned more than $2 billion worldwide.

Hugh Jackman reprises his role as Wolverine in “X-Men Origins: Wolverine,” which opened Friday. Jackman and film producer Lauren Shuler Donner recently sat down for a candid conversation about the new film.

The pair focused on the scene in which Jackman’s character is transformed from a mutant with bony claws that periodically protrude from the backs of his hands into an invincible mutant infused with an indestructible metal called adamantium. The scene marks the birth of a comic-book legend, as the character evolves from Logan into Wolverine.

Watch the scene in which Wolverine is unleashed »

**Hugh Jackman:** I knew this was the birth of the character; this is where we see him in full flight. In the comic book, it’s called “berserker rage.” It’s not really in the English language, but it may be now! The idea that this complete animal has been unleashed is obviously central to the entire story. This battle between the animal and the human is something we all relate to.

**Lauren Shuler Donner:** There were many things he had to do in the tank. One was being lowered into it, and then the needles had to come toward him. Most of those were CGI, so he had to look in specific places where the needles were supposed to be. But he couldn’t hear [director] Gavin [Hood], so they tried all kinds of sounds, speakers—everything. They finally devised this toe method: If Gavin pulled on Hugh’s big toe, it meant the needles were coming; the second toe meant something else; and the last toe meant to rise up. Very sophisticated. *(Laughter)*

**Jackman:** I had it in my head that I needed to be in much better shape—not better shape, but a different kind of shape, a ridiculous shape—because I wanted it to be uncomfortable. I wanted people to feel the way I did when I saw Robert De Niro in “Cape Fear”: Whoa, this guy is dangerous. He’s powerful, he’s dangerous, and he could snap at any moment.

**Donner:** There’s an iconic drawing in the comics of Wolverine emerging from the tank, with the equipment popping off him, his hair wild, and his face filled with rage. We wanted to recreate that image. That’s the image we wanted for the fans.

**Jackman:** I was a little frightened when I watched it. I thought, “Is that me?” [My wife] Deb said, “Hugh, this is ridiculous. I don’t even know who that is.”

LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) — Hugh Jackman became a global star by bringing the legendary comic-book character Wolverine to the screen. Films produced by Lauren Shuler Donner—including every installment in the “X-Men” series—have generated more than $2 billion around the world.

Jackman once again appears as Wolverine in “X-Men Origins: Wolverine,” which debuted Friday. He and Donner recently spoke openly about the movie, focusing on the sequence in which Jackman’s character undergoes a dramatic transformation. Initially, he is Logan, a mutant whose bone claws occasionally extend from the backs of his hands. He then becomes virtually unstoppable after his body is infused with adamantium, an unbreakable metal. The moment marks the definitive creation of the comic-book legend Wolverine.

Watch the sequence where Wolverine is set free »

**Hugh Jackman:** I understood that this moment was the character’s true beginning—the first time audiences see him completely unleashed. In the comics, it is known as “berserker rage.” That phrase was not really part of ordinary English, though perhaps it is now. The scene is about releasing the animal within him, and that is essentially what the whole story explores. Everyone can identify with the struggle between our human side and our animal instincts.

**Lauren Shuler Donner:** Hugh had to perform several actions while inside the tank. He needed to be lowered into it, and then the needles had to move toward him. Because most of the needles were created with CGI, he had to direct his eyes toward specific spots where they would later appear. The problem was that he could not hear director Gavin Hood. The crew experimented with speakers, sounds, and all sorts of other solutions. Eventually, they created an elaborate signaling system using Hugh’s toes: pulling his big toe told him the devices were approaching, another toe communicated a different instruction, and the final toe meant he should rise. It was extremely advanced. *(laughter)*

**Jackman:** I believed I needed to have a much different physique—not simply be fitter, but look almost absurdly muscular—because I wanted viewers to feel uneasy. I was trying to create the same reaction I had when I watched Robert De Niro in “Cape Fear”: the sense that this man is powerful and threatening, and could lose control without warning.

**Donner:** The comics contain a famous image of Wolverine bursting out of the tank in a fury, with objects sticking out of his body and his hair flying everywhere. We wanted to recreate that exact visual for the fans.

**Jackman:** Seeing the finished scene made me slightly nervous. I found myself wondering, “Is that really me?” My wife, Deb, told me, “Hugh, this is absurd. I don’t even recognize that person.”

Hugh Jackman reprises his iconic role as Wolverine in *X-Men Origins: Wolverine*, produced by Lauren Shuler Donner. The film explores Logan’s transformation into the nearly indestructible mutant after his skeleton is infused with adamantium, an exceptionally strong metal.

Jackman regarded this pivotal sequence as Wolverine’s true birth. The agonizing procedure unleashes the character’s primal, animalistic side—his infamous “berserker rage”—and marks the moment when Logan fully becomes the hero audiences recognize.

Filming the transformation was especially demanding. Jackman performed inside a tank and had to react to needles that would be added later through computer-generated effects. Because he could not hear director Gavin Hood’s instructions during filming, the crew devised a practical signaling system: they pulled on Jackman’s toes to cue his movements and reactions. This unusual method enabled him to deliver the intense physical performance required for one of the film’s most technically challenging scenes.
outputs.L4:
In *X-Men Origins: Wolverine*, Logan’s transformation into the adamantium-clawed mutant known as Wolverine is presented as both a physical ordeal and a defining moment for the character. Hugh Jackman and producer Lauren Shuler Donner have described the challenges of filming the sequence, which required Jackman’s intense performance to be combined with extensive computer-generated imagery. The finished scene had to convey unimaginable pain while also showing the birth of the nearly indestructible hero familiar to comic-book audiences.

Because Jackman was positioned inside the transformation tank and surrounded by equipment, communicating with him during filming was difficult. The production team devised an improvised system of toe signals to give him direction while the cameras were rolling. Those cues helped Jackman coordinate his movements and reactions with the visual effects that would later add the machinery, adamantium infusion, and other details of the procedure.

The experiment pushes Logan beyond his ability to remain calm. Once the metal-bonding process is complete, his agony erupts into the “berserker rage” associated with Wolverine in the comics. He breaks free with explosive force, acting less like a controlled soldier than a wounded animal fighting for survival. The sequence therefore serves as more than a visual-effects spectacle: it marks the moment when the legend of Wolverine is born.

At the same time, the scene highlights the conflict that makes the character relatable. Logan possesses extraordinary strength, heightened senses, and violent instincts, but he continually struggles to preserve his humanity. His rage can save him, yet it also threatens to consume him. That tension between human restraint and animal instinct lies at the heart of Wolverine, giving emotional weight to his transformation and shaping the battles—both internal and external—that follow.
